# Third-Party Notices

**Status**: ✅ Implemented — `NOTICE` and `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md` are generated by
`cmd/gen-notices`, regenerated with `just notices`, and enforced by `just check`.

Loom ships two attribution files at the repository root, and both are generated —
never hand-edited:

| File | Covers |
|---|---|
| `NOTICE` | Loom's own copyright, plus the NOTICE files of bundled works, reproduced verbatim |
| `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md` | The full license text of every third-party component in the shipped binaries |

## Why both

They satisfy two different obligations.

Every permissive license in the dependency tree — MIT, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause,
ISC, Apache-2.0, MPL-2.0 — requires the license text and copyright notice to
accompany the distribution. `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md` carries them.

Apache-2.0 §4(d) additionally requires that if a work you redistribute contains a
NOTICE file, its attribution notices are reproduced in your own distribution.
Several dependencies ship one, so `NOTICE` reproduces them.

## What is in scope

The generator lists what is **compiled into the binaries we distribute** —
`loom`, `looms`, `loom-standalone` — using each binary's own release build tags
(`fts5`, and `standalone` for the standalone build).

That is deliberately narrower than the module graph. `go list -m all` resolves
several hundred modules; only a subset reaches a user's machine. Test-only and
build-time modules are not distributed, so listing them would overstate the
obligations and make review harder, not more thorough.

Three properties of the generator matter for accuracy:

- **License text is copied verbatim** from the dependency's own source. Nothing
  classifies or normalizes a license into an SPDX identifier — an identifier is a
  summary, and a summary is not what these licenses require us to ship.
- **A package with its own LICENSE is attributed separately** from its module.
  Some modules vendor subcomponents under a different license; rolling those up to
  the module root would attribute them wrongly.
- **A component whose license cannot be found is a hard error.** The generator
  refuses to write rather than silently omitting it — a missing component is the
  exact compliance failure these files exist to prevent.

## Regenerating

```bash
just notices        # rewrite both files
just notices-check  # fail if they no longer match the dependency tree
```

`notices-check` runs as part of `just check`, so a dependency change that is not
reflected in the notices fails the build in the same way stale generated proto
code does.

## Release packaging

`LICENSE`, `NOTICE`, and `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md` are included in every release
archive alongside the binary. Generating the files is not sufficient on its own —
the obligation is to distribute them *with* the software.

## What this is not

These files are a factual inventory produced from the dependency tree. They are
not a legal opinion, and they cannot detect a dependency that has misdeclared its
own license upstream. Treat a release as the unit of accuracy: regenerate on every
version bump, since the inventory is true of a commit rather than of the product
in general.

## Bundled C libraries

The binaries are built with `CGO_ENABLED=1`. `github.com/mutecomm/go-sqlcipher` is
MIT as a Go module, but compiles in C source from three upstream projects, and its
LICENSE file is a composite covering all of them:

- `mattn/go-sqlite3` (SQLite driver and amalgamation) — MIT
- `sqlcipher/sqlcipher` (encrypted SQLite) — BSD-3-Clause, © 2008 ZETETIC LLC
- `libtom/libtomcrypt` (AES, HMAC, PRNG) — public domain

Module-level license tooling reports only the wrapper's MIT license, so these are
called out explicitly in `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md`.

The Go standard library and runtime are statically linked into every binary and
are distributed under BSD-3-Clause, © 2009 The Go Authors.
